plan.interpretation: After about 4 hours of watching, the learner can reason about Rust ownership, borrowing and lifetimes with confidence, use Result and the ? operator idiomatically, and port their small Go CLI tool to Rust.
assumptions: The learner needs enough Rust syntax and tooling (cargo, structs, enums, match) to follow videos, but this is covered by mapping from Go rather than taught from scratch.
Traits are needed mainly as they relate to error handling, generics bounds and lifetimes, not as a full deep dive.
The ported CLI uses typical pieces: argument parsing (e.g. clap), file or stdin IO, and error propagation.
Videos in English; the learner prefers material aimed at experienced developers coming from Go, C, or C++.

sub_topics.title: Rust orientation for Go developers (cargo, structs, enums, match, Option)
sub_topics.why: Gives the minimum Rust vocabulary and tooling to follow ownership examples, mapped onto Go concepts they already know, without re-teaching variables or loops.

sub_topics.title: Ownership and moves (stack vs heap, move semantics, Copy vs Clone, Drop)
sub_topics.why: Go's GC hides ownership; this learner knows pointers and memory so can grasp move semantics quickly, but must internalize who owns and frees data.

sub_topics.title: Borrowing and references in depth (shared vs mutable borrows, borrow checker rules, common errors)
sub_topics.why: They want depth on the borrow checker; they need to understand aliasing XOR mutability and how to fix typical compiler errors, contrasted with Go pointers and slices.

sub_topics.title: Lifetimes (annotations, elision rules, structs holding references, 'static)
sub_topics.why: Lifetimes are the hardest part for newcomers and are needed for structs and functions that return references, such as parsed CLI config.

sub_topics.title: Traits and generics essentials (impl Trait, trait bounds, From, Display, Error trait)
sub_topics.why: Idiomatic error handling relies on traits such as std::error::Error, From and Display, which are unlike Go interfaces in key ways.

sub_topics.title: Error handling with Result and the ? operator (custom error types, thiserror, anyhow, From conversion)
sub_topics.why: Their Go CLI returns errors everywhere, so they need to translate if err != nil patterns into Result, ?, and custom or anyhow errors.

sub_topics.title: Build a Rust CLI project (clap, file IO, error propagation, ownership in practice)
sub_topics.why: A project-style walkthrough shows ownership, borrowing, lifetimes and Result working together in a tool like the one they are porting.

pool.title: Understanding Rust – Or How to Stop Worrying & Love the Borrow-Checker • Steve Smith • YOW! 2024
pool.description:
This presentation was recorded at YOW! Australia 2024. #GOTOcon #YOW
https://yowcon.com

Steve Smith - Roving Polyglot Developer @TarkaSteve 

ORIGINAL TALK TITLE
Understanding Rust; Or How I Learned to Stop Worrying & Love the Borrow-Checker

RESOURCES
https://bsky.app/profile/tarka.haltcondition.net
https://hachyderm.io/@tarkasteve
https://github.com/tarka
https://www.linkedin.com/in/tarkasteve
https://haltcondition.net

Links
https://emschwartz.me/async-rust-can-be-a-pleasure-to-work-with-without-send-sync-static
https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/send-and-sync.html
https://rust-unofficial.github.io/patterns/idioms/coercion-arguments.html

ABSTRACT
You've seen the Github surveys, you've seen the cool stuff Amazon, Oxide and even Microsoft are working on, and you want to get in on the action. So you fire up an editor and start your first project. And the borrow-checker immediately crushes your hopes and dreams.

If this sounds familiar, this is the talk for you.

Rust can be very welcoming, but it expects you to abide by a few rules that other languages regard as optional
In this talk Steve Smith takes you through some of these core rules and why they exist, drawing comparisons to existing programming techniques such as garbage collection and resource management. He also introduces some of the tools that Rust gives you to work with its rules rather than against them, produce more elegant code, and learn to love the borrow-checker. [...]

pool.title: Build a Rust CLI Tool from Scratch (clap, serde, anyhow) – logscan
pool.description:
Build a real command-line tool in Rust, step by step: logscan, a fast log analyzer with subcommands, colored tables, top-message ranking, highlighted grep, JSON export and unit tests. Along the way we hit a real borrow-checker error (E0515: cannot return value referencing local variable) and fix it the idiomatic way. Every cargo build, run and test is real output.

CHAPTERS:
0:00 Intro
0:06 Why Rust for CLI tools
1:03 Project setup (cargo new, cargo add)
1:53 Step 1: Arguments with clap
3:03 Step 2: Reading files with anyhow
3:59 Step 3: Parsing log lines (zero-copy with lifetimes)
4:45 The borrow checker strikes (E0515)
6:02 Step 4: The fix & colored output
6:58 Step 5: Subcommands & tables
7:43 Step 6: top & grep
8:49 Top messages & validation
9:33 Step 7: JSON output with serde
10:18 Step 8: Unit tests
10:57 Release build
11:22 Recap & next steps

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
- clap derive: Parser, Subcommand, ValueEnum, doc comments as help
- anyhow::Result and .with_context() for readable errors
- Zero-copy parsing with &str and lifetimes
- Understanding and fixing E0515 (who owns the data?)
- colored for terminal colors, comfy-table for tables
- serde + serde_json for JSON output
- #[cfg(test)] unit tests and cargo test
- cargo build --release for a single ~1.5 MB binary

Crates used: clap 4.6, anyhow 1.0, colored 3.1, comfy-table 8.0, serde 1.0, serde_json 1.0
Tested with Rust 1.99.1 (edition 2024).

Quick start:
cargo new logscan && cd logscan
cargo add clap --features derive
cargo add anyhow colored comfy-table serde_json
cargo add serde --features derive
cargo run -- summary app.log

clap docs: https://docs.rs/clap
Rust book, ownership chapter: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership.html

If this helped, like and subscribe to Back to Code for more hands-on programming tutorials!

#Rust #RustLang #CLI #Programming #BorrowChecker

pool.title: Rust for Go Developers: The 6 Things You Actually Need to Learn
pool.description:
Already shipping backends in Go or Spring Boot? Here are the six Rust concepts that actually change how you design a service: ownership and borrowing, Result and Option, shared state, async on Tokio, the production crate stack, and learning from the compiler. Then you get one homework project, a small AI job queue API built with Axum, Tokio, Serde and SQLx.

We follow one document service (upload → API → jobs → worker → AI model) and move its worker to Rust. All logs, timings and job IDs in this video are example data.

Chapters
0:00 We already know how to build this
0:42 1 · Ownership: moves and borrowing
1:35 2 · Result, the ? operator and Option
2:33 3 · Shared state, pools and locks
3:17 4 · Async is not parallel (Tokio)
4:10 5 · Cargo, Axum, Tokio, Serde, SQLx, tracing
5:13 6 · Let the compiler teach you
5:54 Homework: an AI Job Queue API
6:33 Six acceptance criteria
7:05 Keep Go/Spring, add Rust where it fits

Docs: doc.rust-lang.org/book · docs.rs/tokio · docs.rs/axum · docs.rs/sqlx · serde.rs

#rust #golang #backend

pool.title: 🚀 Build a Robust CLI App in Rust with Clap | Rust Programming Tutorial
pool.description:
Are you a Rust developer looking to create professional-grade command-line interface (CLI) applications? Look no further! In this comprehensive tutorial, you'll learn how to build a robust and efficient CLI app using the powerful Clap library🔥🔥🔥.

We'll start by setting up a new Rust project and adding the Clap dependency. Then, we'll dive into defining command-line arguments, parsing and validating user input, handling complex argument structures, and implementing custom validators.

But that's not all! You'll also learn how to handle subcommands, allowing your CLI app to have multiple functionalities. We'll cover generating helpful usage and error messages, ensuring a great user experience.

Error handling and logging are crucial for any production-ready application, and we'll explore best practices for handling errors and logging in Rust. Additionally, we'll discuss testing strategies and techniques for debugging your CLI app.

By the end of this tutorial, you'll have a solid understanding of building robust and maintainable CLI applications in Rust using the Clap library. Whether you're a beginner or an experienced Rust developer, this tutorial will equip you with the skills to create powerful command-line tools.

So, what are you waiting for? Join us on this exciting journey and take your Rust CLI development skills to the next level!. #rustprogramming  #clap  #cli #commandline  #rusttutorial #rust #tutorialyoutube #tutorial #distributedsystems

pool.title: Mastering Error Handling in Rust: From Panics to thiserror & anyhow | with Nathan Stocks
pool.description:
Panics, Results, and error crates—oh my! Confused about how to handle errors in Rust? You’re not alone. Rust gives you powerful tools to manage failure, but using them well takes practice.

In this 1-hour webinar Nathan Stocks will demystify when to panic, how to design clear error types, and why crates like thiserror and anyhow can make your code simpler and safer.

Learn how to architect error handling that scales with your codebase. Perfect for developers ready to move beyond unwrap() and build production-grade Rust applications.

What we'll cover:
- Creating an error vs consuming an error
- Library vs Application error handling
- When to "panic"
- Useful crates: thiserror and anyhow

Repo link: https://github.com/CleanCut/mastering_errors

pool.title: Rust: Generics, Traits, Lifetimes
pool.description:
#rust #generic #traits #lifetime

Generics are like a placeholder to another type. Think of a can with food in it. That can is concrete but the food inside is a generic type. The can have soup, beans, corn, or almost anything else inside it.

We have already been using generics with the `Option` type and `Result` type from the error handling chapter.

Here, we will discover how to use generics with our own functions, structs, and methods.

Traits are used to define behavior in a generic way.

And, finally, you cannot talk about generics without talking about lifetimes. This is Rust feature has probably popped up for you in compiler error messages.

Links

Chapter 17 of the Rust Programming book as it relates to the discussion.
https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch17-02-trait-objects.html

For more complex scenarios involving lifetimes, there’s additional content in the “Rust Reference”. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/trait-bounds.html#trait-and-lifetime-bounds

Then we'll talk about the dreaded/beloved question mark, FromIterator/collect, and some Error stuff.

! - https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.never.html

Sum type - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagged_union
Isomorphism - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism

pool.title: Rust Lifetimes Explained — Finally Make Sense of 'a (2026)
pool.description:
Lifetimes are the #1 reason developers give up on Rust. Not ownership — specifically the moment the compiler asks you to write 'a and you have no idea why.

In this video I explain lifetimes properly — not just the syntax but the mental model that makes everything click. Includes the fresh "loans" mental model from a QCon London 2026 talk that makes borrow checker errors intuitive, plus all the patterns you actually need: elision rules, struct annotations, multiple lifetimes, 'static, and fora.

Title: Idiomatic Error Handling: The ? Operator, Custom Enums, thiserror & anyhow

📌 Overview:
Writing production error handling without boilerplate. Error propagation with the question mark (?) operator, From trait conversions, thiserror for libraries, and anyhow for applications.

- Use anyhow::Result and Context for application-level code to attach rich diagnostic context to errors
